task.name: Test processes a dev agent spawns outlive the sprint that started them and go on consuming the host indefinitely
task.story_text:
## Observed

Test processes a dev agent spawns inside its sandbox outlive the sprint that created them, and go
on consuming the machine indefinitely.

Story `issue-2284`'s dev agent ran the project's own suite four times while working, three of them
with `pytest -n auto --dist worksteal`, concurrently. Those invocations never terminated. Thirteen
hours after the sprint completed and its worktree was deleted, the machine still carried:

```
40 processes, ~321% CPU total
parent 4129   13:20:23  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py::...
parent 68119  13:56:07  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q -n auto --dist
parent 71222  13:51:50  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q -n auto --dist
parent 85040  13:41:11  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q
```

The parents were alive, not orphaned children of a reaped tree, and every worker executed from
`.forge/worktrees/issue-2284/.venv` — a path that no longer exists, held open by the running
processes.

The effect was not confined to wasted CPU. Every gate run on this host afterwards competed with
roughly three cores of dead test workers: a `make gate` that normally completes in about 55
seconds took 181, and a wall-clock timeout test failed inside it while passing three times out of
three when run alone. That failure was read as a possible regression in an unrelated story. Every
run duration recorded during those thirteen hours — the same durations adaptive limits derive dev
timeouts from — was measured against a host under load that nothing accounted for.

## Expected

Work a sprint starts should not outlive the sprint. A story's agent runs inside a sandbox with a
worktree, a virtualenv and a budget, all of which end when the story does; a process it spawned is
part of that same envelope and should end with it, whether the story succeeded, failed, or was
stopped.

The failure is quiet in a way that matters. A leaked process produces no artifact, no cost record
and no log line, so nothing in the run reports it and nothing in a later run knows it is there.
What it changes instead is every timing measurement taken afterwards on the same host — which is
the input the system uses to decide how long work should be allowed to take. A leak that only
wasted CPU would be a nuisance; one that silently biases the measurements the scheduler learns
from is a correctness problem for everything measured while it persists.

That an agent runs the suite at all is reasonable and worth keeping. That it can run it several
times concurrently, each fanning out across every core, inside an environment already running
under the coordinator's own parallelism, is a resource decision nobody made — the agent has no way
to know what else is executing, so the bound has to come from the side that does.

## Diagnosis

- **Observed symptom:** pytest processes spawned by a dev agent remain running and consuming CPU
  long after the sprint that started them has completed and its worktree has been removed.
- **Evidence:** four `pytest` parents with elapsed times of 13h20m–13h56m, PPIDs alive, and 40
  associated workers totalling ~321% CPU, all executing `.forge/worktrees/issue-2284/.venv/bin/python`
  after that worktree was deleted. Three carried `-n auto --dist worksteal`. The sprint that
  spawned them had completed and landed via #2285.
- **Ruled out:** not the 21-day-old orphaned `codex exec` pair from another project — those are
  idle, 13 minutes of CPU across 21 days, and unrelated.
- **Ruled out:** not a worktree-cleanup failure. The worktree was removed; the processes held the
  freed inode open, which is why they remained visible under a path that no longer resolves.
- **Confirmed cause:** processes started by an agent inside its sandbox are not part of anything
  the sprint tears down at story end, so a subprocess that does not exit on its own persists
  without limit.
- **Affected code path:** sandbox process supervision and story teardown.
- **Fix-success criterion:** a process a story's agent starts does not outlive the story, whatever
  the story's outcome, and a process that has to be terminated at teardown is recorded so the run
  shows it happened. The suite remains runnable by an agent; what it cannot do is leave work
  behind.

handoff.summary: P1 (macOS prune ineffective): the lease prune read the whole process table in one bulk KERN_PROC_ALL sysctl and, whenever that read was unavailable, fell back to considering every live process — silently degrading into the full environment scan it was added to remove. That bulk read never failed on this host (0/200, even under process churn), so the cliff was invisible here while the reviewer's host hit it as 564-of-564. Start times now come one process at a time via process_tree.process_info, the same reader the tracker and identity checks already depend on and which validates its struct offsets against ground truth at import; it has no all-or-nothing branch. ProcessInfo gained started_at (epoch seconds) alongside fingerprint — the former orders a process against a wall clock, the latter only ever compares against itself. The prune also got sharper: a process the kernel refuses to describe is another user's, and its environment is refused for the same reason (measured: 0 of 161 refused-bsdinfo processes had a readable environ; 80 of 80 readable ones did), and a lease can only be held by our own descendant, so those are skipped rather than read. Result: 544 live -> 2 candidates, 1.1ms overhead over subprocess.run. P2 (Linux unpruned): fixed rather than documented — the same reader now dates Linux processes from /proc/stat btime + starttime/HZ, verified in a python:3.12-slim container (9 live -> 1 candidate, the correct one, 0.27ms). That container run also caught a defect this branch had introduced: Linux keeps a zombie's /proc entry while macOS refuses to describe an exited process, so a killed escapee read as gone on one platform and as a surviving leak on the other; forge running as pid 1 in a container never reaps its own orphans, so every clean teardown there would have been recorded as a leak that survived. _parse_stat now reports state Z as gone. P2 (untested migration): _migrate_v24_to_v25's source backfill now has tests asserting its output, that already-sourced entries are untouched, and that empty/malformed shapes survive.

story_deviations: The bulk-sysctl fast path was removed rather than repaired. Retrying it would have kept a branch whose failure mode is silent degradation to a full scan, and the per-process reader is fast enough (0.27-1.1ms) that the fast path bought little.

One of my own tests from the previous iteration asserted a host-specific candidate count; it now asserts the correctness condition instead, which is checkable on any host. Two tests in that group were racy — they re-enumerated the process table after computing candidates, so a process born in between looked dropped — and now snapshot the table first.

handoff.summary: Advisory pass on the carried P2 (zombie counted as a live group member on Linux). Measured it first, which changed the fix twice. It was not Linux-specific: macOS listed the corpse too, and killpg's signal-0 probe reports a group holding one as alive on both platforms — so a teardown that worked waited out its full KILL_GRACE_SECONDS and was then recorded as survivors that outlived the run, which is what forge running as pid 1 in a container sees for every child it kills. Fixed by making the readers agree by construction rather than by keeping two parsers in step: group_members_checked now filters membership through process_tree (the reader every descendant check already settles on, extracted the raw platform enumeration into _enumerate_group), and _await_empty_group now prefers that completed enumeration over the probe via a new _group_is_empty, falling back to the probe only where enumeration is unavailable. Both platforms settle in 0.00s instead of 2.0s and record killed_survivors/completed=True. The finding's literal fix — the state-Z exclusion in process_group._parse_proc_stat — was implemented, verified in a Linux container, found to cause a regression, and reverted: that parser also feeds _leader_fingerprint, whose caller needs the opposite answer, because a corpse still occupies its pid and its start time is the proof the pgid was not recycled. Removing that proof made _identity_verdict decline the record (a corpse answers signal-0, so the leader branch is still taken) and would have left the group's live descendants running — the exact case the reaper exists for. Both behaviours are now pinned by tests and the asymmetry is documented at each parser.

handoff.summary: P1, second cycle on group_members_checked, so I changed the structure rather than patching again. The defect: membership was established from the platform enumeration and then refined by a second, independently fallible per-process reader (process_tree.process_info) while keeping the first read's `enumerated` flag — so when that second reader failed for every member, a live group reported itself empty AND fully enumerated, and _release_group treated it as clean and dropped the reaper sidecar without signalling the survivors. Fixed by having one read answer both questions: macOS carries p_stat in the same kinfo_proc record as pid and start time (verified SRUN=2 live, SZOMB=5 after a kill, offset 36), and Linux carries state in the same /proc/<pid>/stat line, so group_members_checked now enumerates per platform and either succeeds or reports enumerated=False. process_tree is no longer consulted for membership at all. A darwin record the layout cannot parse now also yields enumerated=False rather than being silently skipped. _parse_proc_stat returns the state instead of acting on it, because its two callers need opposite answers — membership drops a corpse, _leader_fingerprint keeps one, since a corpse still occupies its pid and that is the proof the pgid was not recycled (removing that proof in an earlier cycle left live descendants running). Verified on macOS and in a Linux-as-pid-1 container: live member survives the descendant reader failing; failed group read gives ({}, False) and release retains the sidecar as retained_for_reaper/completed=False; zombie excluded; zombie leader still fingerprints. P2: workspace setup/install commands now thread a teardown collector through _run_setup_split and _create_workspace into state via source=workspace_setup (gate_run 0, since no gate has run that early), closing the last recording hole; the collector is forwarded only when supplied, so no existing call shape or mock assertion changed.

Propagating enumerated=False from the filter would have kept two readers and left the same class of bug reachable whenever only some members failed the second read.

reviews.summary: [openai-gpt-5.5-cli] The leak-containment behavior is covered, but the submitted macOS lease-pruning guard fails because short-command release still scans the full process table. | [deepseek-deepseek-reasoner-api] The change closes the #2309 leak at every spawn site: release now verifies the group emptied on clean exit and kills survivors/escapees, teardown facts ride out of every runner and shell into the audit record, the reaper gains lease + observed-descendant signals for SIGKILLed sprints, and real-subprocess lifecycle coverage pins each failure mode. | [google-gemini-3.5-flash-api] Fabulous process group and descendant containment fix that ensures no spawned test processes outlive dev runner invocations or gate/sprint lifecycles.

findings.description: On macOS, a lease opened for a short command still produces a candidate set containing every live process on the host, and the focused lifecycle test fails with 564 of 564 processes considered.

The reader-side migrations _migrate_v24_to_v25 (source backfill on gate_process_teardowns) and _migrate_v23_to_v24 (process_teardown on cost.agents) are exercised only indirectly, through test_pre_v24_records_read_back_as_did_not_say which chains v23 to v25 for cost.agents only, so the gate_process_teardowns 'source' backfill has no test asserting its actual output.

The Linux lease candidate set is deliberately unpruned, so every shell-command release reads /proc/<pid>/environ for the entire process table, while the macOS path prunes by start time and is the only branch a test asserts on.

findings.description: On Linux, group_members_checked still counts a zombie as a live group member because its /proc stat parser lacks the state-Z exclusion that process_tree._parse_stat gained in the same branch, so the two parsers now disagree about whether an exited process is gone.

ac_verification.evidence: src/theforge/process_group.py:385-437 stamps a lease, registers the process group, starts descendant tracking, and releases the group through teardown on every exit path; src/theforge/process_group.py:549-613 kills in-group survivors and escaped descendants before returning. The runner call sites consume this path in src/theforge/runners/runner_claude.py:818-935, src/theforge/runners/runner_codex.py:731-744, and src/theforge/runners/runner_gemini.py:161-173. finding_registry.description: On macOS, a lease opened for a short command still produces a candidate set containing every live process on the host, and the focused lifecycle test fails with 564 of 564 processes considered.

The reader-side migrations _migrate_v24_to_v25 (source backfill on gate_process_teardowns) and _migrate_v23_to_v24 (process_teardown on cost.agents) are exercised only indirectly, through test_pre_v24_records_read_back_as_did_not_say which chains v23 to v25 for cost.agents only, so the gate_process_teardowns 'source' backfill has no test asserting its actual output.

The Linux lease candidate set is deliberately unpruned, so every shell-command release reads /proc/<pid>/environ for the entire process table, while the macOS path prunes by start time and is the only branch a test asserts on.

On Linux, group_members_checked still counts a zombie as a live group member because its /proc stat parser lacks the state-Z exclusion that process_tree._parse_stat gained in the same branch, so the two parsers now disagree about whether an exited process is gone.

On macOS, a transient proc_pidinfo failure for every member of a live process group makes group_members_checked return empty members with enumerated=True, so _release_group treats the group as clean and drops its reaper sidecar without ever signalling the survivors.

The workspace setup/install commands (create/setup_command/install) run through _run_shell without a teardown_out collector, so if a setup command leaves workers behind they are killed at release but the run's record never says it happened.

When workspace creation recovers from a branch collision by reusing a registered worktree, a setup command that leaves a process behind is torn down without any workspace_setup entry reaching the run record.
When the sprint baseline workspace setup command fails after leaking a process that teardown kills, the returned baseline error record omits process_teardowns even though the collector was populated.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
